Here are some practical things to look for when shopping for a new electric guitar, based on what we discussed before:

- Body, construction and weight: try different body shapes (single-cut Les Paul vs contoured Strat) and notice how they sit and feel. Les Paul–style guitars tend to be heavier with a set neck and a carved top; Strats are typically contoured and lighter with a bolt‑on neck — pick what’s comfortable for long playing.

- Neck shape and feel: play the neck up and down the fretboard to see which profile and radius suit your hand. Comfort affects technique and speed.

- Pickups and tonal options: check the pickup configuration and whether there’s coil‑tap / coil‑splitting (if available). Coil‑splitting gives you more tonal flexibility, letting a guitar cover brighter single‑coil‑like tones as well as humbucker warmth.

- Tone and genre fit: listen for the core tonal character. Les Paul–type guitars give a warm, rich tone with strong sustain (great for rock, hard rock, metal and thicker rhythms). If you play fingerpicking or acoustic‑style parts, try the guitar unplugged and plugged in to judge clarity.

- Setup and string choice: ask about string gauge and consider trying heavier strings if you plan to use lower or open tunings (open D was discussed before — heavier strings help with low tunings). Also check action, neck relief, and whether the guitar intonates and stays in tune.

- Playability tests: play open chords, single‑note lines, and the kinds of parts you’ll actually play (including any alternate tunings you use). Listen for fret buzz, check sustain, and test bending and tapping if relevant.

- Electronics and amp interaction: plug into an amp you know (or bring your pedal/amp settings) and try the guitar through clean and overdriven tones to hear how pickups respond and how controls behave.

- Hardware and build quality: inspect tuners, bridge, fret ends, and wiring. Make sure tuners hold tune and the hardware feels solid.

- Practical extras: check the case or gig bag, warranty, and whether the shop will do a setup or let you take it to your tech.

If you want, tell me whether you’re leaning toward a Les Paul or a Strat, or what styles you play, and I can suggest specific things to prioritize while trying them out.

Here are practical, evidence-backed tips to get better results with your slow cooker, drawn from the recipes and yogurt/vegan notes you’ve been discussing:

1. Layer and size wisely
- Put dense vegetables (potatoes, carrots) and tougher cuts of meat on the bottom so they cook evenly. Don’t overfill the pot—leave some headspace so heat circulates.

2. Sear meats (when applicable)
- For stews or pulled pork, sear the meat in a skillet first for better browning and deeper flavor before transferring to the slow cooker.

3. Use the right amount of liquid
- Slow cooking needs liquid, but not too much; the lid traps steam so reduce liquid compared with stovetop recipes unless you want a soupy result.

4. Manage cook times and temperature
- Use Low for long, gentle cooking (tenderizes proteins and melds flavors); High shortens time but can make some ingredients fall apart. Add delicate items (peas, zucchini, quick-cooking beans) near the end so they don’t disintegrate.

5. Handle dairy and thickeners at the end
- Add milk, cream, yogurt, or coconut milk toward the end of cooking to prevent curdling. If you want a thicker sauce, finish on the stove to reduce or stir in a cornstarch slurry at the end.

6. For vegetarian/vegan dishes
- Slow cookers are great for lentil curries, roasted-vegetable stews, and other plant-based one-pots—use sturdier legumes/veg that hold up to long cooking. Consider coconut or soy bases for creaminess.

7. Making slow-cooker yogurt (and cashew-based yogurt)
- Basic slow-cooker yogurt approach: heat milk (or alternative base) then incubate with live cultures to set. For cashew yogurt: soak cashews thoroughly, then blend until completely smooth. Strain using a nut-milk bag or fine mesh/cheesecloth if you want an extra-smooth texture. Add flavorings/sweeteners (vanilla, cinnamon, honey or maple) after incubating.

8. Flavoring and sweetening ideas
- Try vanilla, cinnamon, fruit purées, maple syrup, or honey (or maple/agave for vegan) to finish yogurt or savory dishes; add fresh herbs at the end for brightness in stews.

9. Small tests and adjustments
- If trying new ingredients (e.g., freeze-dried or plant bases), test small batches first and tweak soaking/blending times or liquid ratios based on texture and flavor.
